title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator Suite for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a reproducible synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator suite to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM configuration generator on operationally framed intent→configuration tasks. The confirmatory paired design used N=300 intent tasks across four intent categories (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies) with a sealed preregistration. The declared model was gpt-5-mini; the deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail) and analyzed with a paired test. Results: baseline (single‑pass) 299/300 passes, guarded (GVR) 300/300 passes; paired difference = 0.00333 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Confirmatory conclusion: on this curated synthetic task set and validator semantics both methods attained near‑ceiling pass rates and the preregistered primary hypothesis (that the GVR pipeline increases pass rate materially) was not supported. We report the full preregistered plan, execution manifest, analysis artifacts, and limitations; code, task generator, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis outputs are archived in the execution bundle. Exploratory diagnostics show only one discordant pair, preventing robust failure‑mode clustering. We discuss interpretation (ceiling effect, construct validity of the validator, and external validity limits) and release the benchmark artifacts to enable broader community evaluation.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and repair. Prior work shows LLM drafts can contain syntax/topology/semantic errors and that verifier‑assisted repair can improve outcomes in focused case studies [surveys & empirical reports summarized in Related Work]. Research gap. There is no widely accepted, machine‑checkable, reproducible NetOps benchmark that pairs realistic task families, deterministic validators, and a sealed confirmatory protocol to compare generator architectures or interventions. Contribution. We present (1) a publicly archived synthetic benchmark generator and canonical intent→configuration task family, (2) a deterministic validator suite expressing machine‑checkable safety/correctness constraints, (3) a sealed preregistered paired experiment (N=300) comparing a GVR pipeline to a frozen single‑pass generator, and (4) the completed execution and analysis artifacts showing near‑ceiling performance on the curated tasks and discussing implications for evaluation design and external validity.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and empirical studies have documented active research on LLMs for NetOps, the promise of intent‑based translation, and the documented failure modes of naive LLM generation (hallucination, syntax/topology errors) as well as the potential of generate–validate–repair architectures to reduce errors [see collected surveys and empirical reports]. Security analyses highlight prompt injection and adversarial prompt risks relevant to operational workflows. Work that combines LLM generation with formal or deterministic verification (e.g., Verified Prompt Programming and localized verifier feedback) demonstrates proof‑of‑concept improvements in limited scenarios but remains limited in scale and diversity of tasks. These findings motivated a preregistered, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison focused on operationally meaningful validator semantics rather than only language‑level correctness.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The preregistered plan (study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) specified a paired confirmatory hypothesis H1: GVR improves per‑task validator pass rate versus a single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks (α=0.05). The task generator created synthetic tasks across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies) with controlled difficulty metadata. Model and orchestration. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (as recorded in the execution manifest). Execution adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Baseline condition used the shared initial single generation; guarded condition applied the GVR pipeline (generate→deterministic validation→at most one automated repair invocation). Validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) enforced snapshot, machine‑checkable constraints (required command sequences, preserve fields, make‑before‑break constraints) and returned binary pass/fail plus structured diagnostics. Seeds, generation prompts, and all provider traces were preserved. Sampling and budget. Planned N=300 paired tasks, maximum model calls 600; actual model_calls_used=301 (300 shared initial + 1 repair invocation). Analysis plan. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary analysis used the preregistered paired binary executor (exact McNemar two‑sided test) and paired bootstrap percentile CI (10k resamples, seed 1729). Missingness, exclusion and contamination rules were preregistered and applied deterministically.
sections.results: Execution summary. The preregistered run completed without technical exclusions: completed_pair_count=300, model_calls_used=301 (one automated repair stage invoked once). Confirmatory outcome (primary): baseline_success_count=299/300 (0.9967), guarded_success_count=300/300 (1.0000). Paired contingency: n11=299, n10=1 (guarded only), n01=0 (baseline only), n00=0. Estimate (guarded−baseline) = 0.00333. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Interpretive summary. Both conditions achieved near‑ceiling validator pass rates on the curated tasks. The single observed discordant pair favored guarded; overall the difference is numerically tiny and statistically non‑significant under the preregistered test. Exploratory diagnostics. Planned exploratory analyses (failure‑mode clustering, per‑cluster paired summaries, reproducibility checks) were run; because only one discordant outcome occurred there is insufficient data to characterize robust failure clusters. All raw responses, validator traces, provider call traces, manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion: Scientific interpretation. The confirmatory result indicates that for the curated synthetic tasks and the chosen deterministic validator semantics both a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator and the GVR pipeline produced operationally valid configurations at near‑ceiling rates. This outcome should not be read as evidence that GVR is unnecessary for broader NetOps deployments. Alternative explanations: (1) ceiling effect — the selected synthetic tasks and/or validator rules may be insufficiently challenging or may align closely with patterns the model was able to reproduce; (2) construct validity — the deterministic validator encodes specific snapshot semantics (finite required sequences and preserved fields) that may not capture all operational risks (runtime interactions, vendor idiosyncrasies, performance implications); (3) coverage — synthetic topologies (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) do not equal production heterogeneity. Operational implication. The benchmark and deterministic validator are intended as a reproducible evaluation substrate; achieving near‑ceiling results highlights the need for (a) broader task difficulty ranges, (b) richer validator semantics (temporal/in‑flight checks, multi‑device stateful simulations), and (c) multi‑model and multi‑vendor cross‑validation before production claims. Relation to prior work. Our findings complement prior case studies where verifier feedback improved generator outputs in specific tasks; here, when validator semantics align tightly with the generator’s capabilities, single‑pass generation may already meet the expressed constraints.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a reproducible synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator suite and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a GVR pipeline versus a single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 tasks. Both methods achieved near‑perfect validator pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300) and the preregistered primary hypothesis of a material GVR improvement was not supported on this task set. The result emphasizes the importance of benchmark design: ceiling effects and validator construct limitations can mask meaningful differences. We release the task generator, validator, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts to enable the community to broaden the benchmark (harder tasks, stateful validators, multi‑model comparisons) and to study where GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value. All artifacts referenced in this paper are archived in the execution bundle described in the manuscript evidence manifest and can be independently verified using the supplied manifests and hashes.

Models and tooling. The declared LLM used for generation was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version in execution/model_configuration.json). The experiment used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter/orchestration framework to implement both the baseline single‑pass generation and the guarded generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline. The deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) and performed machine‑checkable snapshot validation of generated configurations. Master prompt and autonomy. The exact immutable initial master prompt used to initiate the autonomous research run is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and is referenced rather than reproduced here per archive practice. Human role and pre‑lock development. A human Research Director selected the high‑level topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the scope prior to the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock collaborative development occurred to build infrastructure and rehearsal code; those pre‑lock development runs were explicitly excluded from the final empirical evidence unless recreated under the post‑lock pipeline. We confirm no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Preregistration and procedures. The confirmatory study plan, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, failed_call_treatment, stopping rules, and analysis executor were frozen before observing outcomes (see preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1). Data and artifacts. All generated tasks, shared initial generations, guarded repair traces, validator outputs, execution logs, and analysis outputs are archived in the execution bundle with recorded SHA‑256 artifact hashes and are referenced throughout the manuscript. Provider and compute. The run used hosted model responses (provider recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). Maximum model_call budget and actual usage were preregistered; model_calls_used=301 (300 shared initial calls + 1 repair call). Deviations and restarts. No technical restarts or post‑preregistration design changes were applied to influence outcomes; the execution manifest records zero failed episodes and no post‑hoc modifications. Limitations in disclosure. This Disclosure Statement describes the autonomous post‑lock execution. It does not claim that the project was autonomous from inception; pre‑lock infrastructure development and human topic selection occurred and are explicitly documented in the evidence bundle.
limitations: Construct validity: The deterministic validator encodes specific snapshot safety/correctness semantics; it does not model runtime, dynamic protocol interactions, vendor‑specific execution idiosyncrasies, or traffic‑level performance impacts.

External validity: Tasks were synthetically generated and abstracted (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models); results do not imply equivalent performance on heterogeneous production networks or on private customer configurations.

Ceiling effect: Near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) indicate limited headroom in the selected task set, constraining the ability to detect practical differences between methods.
Model and scope limits: Only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or larger/smaller variants without further multi‑model experiments.
Failure‑mode analysis: Because only one discordant outcome occurred, exploratory failure clustering and robust subgroup inference are underpowered and therefore inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: While all artifacts, manifests, and hashes are archived, reproducing exact hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in the execution manifest.
